maintopic: RADIO BROADCASTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this might be an appropriate moment to refer again to the designation of the introducer of this bill. This bill appears on the order paper in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and my right hon. friend who has just introduced the bill (Sir George Perley) is either the Prime Minister or the acting Prime Minister, he cannot be both. I see no reason why bills should not appear on the order paper in the name of whoever may be the acting Prime Minister if he is responsible for the measure so that the records may be complete. I looked up the votes and proceedings of the house to see what had been done in 1919 when Sir Robert Borden was unfortunately indisposed and unable to be present in the house for a time. Sir George Foster was the acting Prime Minister at the time and I notice that bills and resolutions were introduced in Sir George's name when he was the acting Prime Minister. It may be the modesty of my right hon. friend which has caused him to omit putting in his own name when acting as Prime Minister, I have no doubt he has been appointed acting Prime Minister by order in council of the cabinet and that he is the acting Prime Minister. Measures that are brought in by my right hon. friend should be in his name. Further on, on the order paper, we have a notice for adjournment and it again is in the name of the Prime Minister. My right hon. friend did tell us the other day that the Prime Minister was keeping in touch with matters in the house, but I submit that that is not sufficient. The procedure with respect to public measures where it is of permanent record should not be designated otherwise than as is strictly accurate. I mention this again though I do not want to make any particular point of it except to see that the proceedings of parliament and particularly of this house are kept and of record in the regular way.

speechtext:
I am quite
prepared to abide by the ruling of the Speaker, but I should be surprised if his honour ruled against me in regard to this motion, which is a substantive motion, and I am speaking immediately to it. However, I will relieve my hon. friend's anxiety by saying that I am not going to speak at any length. The point to which I wish to direct particular attention is this, that the public interest is the interest to which this parliament should give first consideration. I submit that the longer we delay permitting the public to express itself with respect to the government that is to carry on the business of this country for the next few years, the more we are going to prejudice the public interest in Canada. Hon. gentlemen know very well that until a general election is over it will not be possible for business to settle down in any normal way, nor will it be possible to hope for the normal and natural revival which we trust will come after a general election. I say this irrespective of the particular government that may be returned. The other day I heard someone refer to the presidential election year in the United States as a year in which very little progress is made with business, because of uncertainty as to what may result at the end of the election. Unfortunately next year will be the presidential year in the United States, there will be uncertainty there, from which this country will suffer in part. But if we are to wait until after midsummer and on into the fall of this year before the general election takes place business in Canada is going to be very materially prejudiced.
One pretext after another has been used by the government for continuing itself in office. After the by-elections of last fall, when we had what was spoken of as a miniature general election and government candidates were not only defeated but slaughtered everywhere, we were told that it was impossible to have a general election then because voters' lists were not ready. When parliament reassembled I spoke about the lists and my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) told us that the lists would not be ready until about April 15, but

Easter Adjournment

that they would be ready by that time. To-day is April 15. I think at that time the country had reason to hope that the lists being ready by April 15 it might expect a general election towards the end of April or early in May. Now the revision of the lists is being made, and I suppose we shall be told later that until the revision is completed we cannot hope to have a general election. The revision will probably take until July or August. That means that it will possibly be some time in September when the new government that is elected assumes office or the present government is confirmed in office.
Whether hon. gentlemen opposite are returned to office or another government is elected, it will take some little time after the election before the new administration whichever it may be, can begin to introduce and enforce its policies for the improvement of employment, the relief of unemployment, the furtherance of trade and the like. Also until after there has been a general election there will not be opportunity for any government satisfactorily to negotiate agreements with respect to trade. Until after a general election nothing can be done, for example, with respect to the revision of the Canada-United Kingdom agreements, nor is it likely that anything can be done satisfactorily with respect to a reciprocal trade agreement with the United States. Nor is it probable that any government in Europe, America or Asia will negotiate with the administration in this country until after the people have spoken. That means that with respect to the bringing about of such changes in conditions as can be effected through negotiations with other countries all this will be delayed until on into the fall. Being delayed that long means that winter will be approaching, and that the effect of any arrangements will not be felt until the year following. It will be too late for new markets. I think it is most unfortunate that such should be the case. The election should have been held last year, as hon. gentLemen well know. Now we are prolonging the session, not with a view of suiting the needs or interests of the country, or even considering the interests and the wishes of parliament, but simply to enable a moribund government to perpetuate itself longer in office in the hope that, not yet being able to win as far as they can see yet, something may turn up before the last moment arrives which will help to save the day.
I protest again against this delay because t means that we shall come back at the ..atter part of May, be held here possibly

through the greater part of the summer, and then there will be further delay before the general election. I think there is material enough, with the business on the order paper and what we have now before us in the form of reports, to enable us to continue after a recess of a few days, and thereby expedite the moment at which the people will come into their real and long denied right of expressing their wushes in a general election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes).
On April the 11th, page 2622 of the debates, the hon. Minister of Finance, answering a question from the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell), said:
I find that the master of the Royal Canadian Mint, acting on behalf of the Royal Mint at London, has received a quantity which he has arranged to be distributed through the ...
The names of five English Canadian firms are then given.
I do not know what the authority of the Finance minister in this matter may be, as far as the master of the Royal Canadian Mint is concerned, but may I ask the minister if he will be kind enough to see the master of the Canadian Mint and make sure that the latter will extend to French Canadian firms the same privileges as those granted English Canadian ones.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE KING'S SILVER JUBILEE
subtopic: DISTRIBUTION OP MEDALS IN COMMEMORATION OF EVENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will appreciate that the Master of the Mint is not in the habit of merchandizing, and the distribution of the silver jubilee medals was not a merchandizing proposition. He was acting upon the request of the royal mint in London to distribute
medals for sale in a quantity which it was felt the market would consume, I do not quite understand how the question would arise as to having distribution through French Canadian firms, because my hon. friend will appreciate that those who are distributing the medals are incorporated companies, all of them. I believe it would be fair to assume that those companies would have French speaking employees and French speaking shareholders. If the companies were French I take it, conversely, that English employees and English shareholders would not be debarred.
I do not know that the subject could be elucidated any further by making inquiries from the master of the mint, although I shall be happy to do so. In conversation with him he advised me there1 were now some people desirous of distributing the medals and taking advantage of the advertising, which is being paid for by those companies who have the distribution in hand, although when approached by the master of the mint in the first place they were not interested.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of Saturday, April 13. This article makes a brief reference to the interruption by the minister of the speech of the financial critic of the opposition (Mr. Ralston) on the budget, and states:
But it is not hard to guess what Colonel Ralston intended to say. He was about to make a statement that after Judge Fullerton made a statement in Halifax last summer defending the Canadian National from the attacks of Mr. Beatty and the other advocates of "unification" (a blessed word this, so different from "amalgamation"!) he was told by the government not to offend Mr. Beatty and the government in this respect again.
It will be remembered that at the time various ministerial newspapers were scandalized at Judge Fullerton's temerity in talking back. They were, it now appears, reflecting the views of Mr. Bennett and Dr. Manion.
I should like to know if that statement is founded either on fantasy or fact.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subtopic: DENIAL OF STATEMENT THAT GOVERNMENT HAD INTERVENED TO INFLUENCE OR SUPPRESS DISCUSSION BY JUDGE FULLERTON OF RAILWAY PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to let me know that he was going to ask this question and I checked up the statement made by Judge Fullerton last year in the railways and shipping committee. As a matter of fact, I had already done this as other newspapers had taken somewhat the same attitude with regard to the statement made this year in the committee. I should like to quote a couple of sentences from the statement made in the committee last year by Judge Fullerton, I am glad to have this opportunity as I do not like being painted as a traitor to my country, as I have been in articles of this sort. Judge Fullerton is reported on page five of the minutes of proceedings of the committee held last year as follows:
There is one other matter to which I must
refer. Reference was made by a member of the committee to public addreses delivered by

C.N.R.-Refunding
the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I was asked to comment on these. It had not been my intention, for reasons which I shall later state, to refer to these speeches or to the efforts which are presently being carried on to promote the idea of amalgamation or, failing that, unified management of the two great railway systems, but since the matter has been raised in the committee I feel it my duty to make a brief statement.
Later on he speaks of having sent out some propaganda to the employees of the Canadian National Railways, and he says:
The results, it is believed, have been a strengthening of the morale of the employees. There is, however, a different attitude to be taken towards public discussions of these questions on the part of the trustees.
And again:
The trustees of the Canadian National Railways felt that if they were to carry out the obligation thus imposed upon them by parliament itself, they could not, consistently with their duty, enter into any argument or discussion in reference to subject matters which were expressly forbidden by parliament itself,-
He then goes on to state that section 27 of the Railway Act forbade such discussion and the trustees did not feel that they had any right to discuss the matter. On the following page he says:
The trustees have by their oath of office assumed the responsibility of carrying out on their part the terms of the act of parliament, and any attempt by them to publicly answer propaganda urging amalgamation or unified control might, and probably would, place them in a false position.
There might well be an even more serious result. The essence of all cooperative plans is goodwill and earnestness towards the accomplishment of the object in view. The public controversy of the nature indicated, as well as being improper on the part of the trustees, would, because of its futility, raise obstacles in the way of the plan of cooperation.
What I am seeking to do is to make clear the reasons which, even if I were minded to do so, prevent me from combating propaganda in a battle of words.
A little later the hon. member for Van-couver-iBurrard (Mr. Hanbury) and the horn, member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) complimented Judge Fullerton on his statement. Apparently this is the reason why Judge Fullerton has not been making any replies. I make the positive statement that Judge Fullerton has never at any time been instructed by me or the government, to my knowledge, to refrain from making any speech which he might choose to make. I say here publicly that Judge Fullerton is as much at liberty to make any speech as is Mr. (Beatty. The statement made in the Winnipeg Free Press is false in every word and line and merely illustrates the general perverted attitude of the editor of that paper.
I am not referring to the representatives of that paper located in Ottawa, but when the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press writes upon political matters he never tells the truth if a falsehood will serve.

speechtext:
I do not want to enter into any long discussion of this matter, but I do not hold the Minister of Railways responsible, in connection with the question I am going to discuss, because he has repeatedly declared on the floor of the house that he has nothing to do with the administration of the Canadian National Railways-the whole thing rests with the trustees and the management of the road. In justice to my constituents, and in view of the resolution adopted a few days ago by the county council of Bonaventure, I must protest once more against

C .N.R.-Refunding
the policy followed in that constituency. First of all, as regards the shops, it is claimed that the work is being removed gradually from the shops at New Carlisle and the day is not far distant when those shops will be closed entirely. A good deal of the work that could be done there is being done at Camp'bell-ton or Moncton, to the great disadvantage of the railway men who have settled at New Carlisle. It is unjust to these men who have their residences there and have settled in the district. They are being turned away gradually, one after another, and the day is not distant when the shops will disappear entirely. The people of that constituency were under the impression, when the Gaspe railway was taken over, that what work could be done not only in Bonaventure but in the Gaspe district would be done in the shops at New Carlisle, and these men have protested that this is not being followed out. Work that could be done at New Carlisle is being done either at Campbellton or at Moncton. That is the first point.
The second point of complaint is as regards the terminus at Matapedia. When the Chaleur bay railway was built, with provincial subsidy, it was stated in the act that the terminus of the railway would be in the province of Quebec on the banks of the Restigouche river. For thirty or thirty-five years the terminus was at Matapedia in the province of Quebec, but the road was subsidized by the dominion and ultimately taken over by the Canadia National Railways, and they have transferred the terminus from Matapedia to Campbellton, New Brunswick. When the train reaches Matapedia it goes back eastward thirteen miles to Campbellton where the terminus is now located. The whole population of Matapedia valley and the county of Bonaventure, irrespective of party, have protested time and again against this action. The hon. member for Matane (Mr. Larue), a strong supporter of the government at the present time, as he has been for the last five years, attended a meeting held at Matapedia where I was present and he protested strongly against this change being made. It is an injustice to that part of the county and should be remedied. The government may say that the administration has been handed over to the Canadian National Railways, and so on and so on; but when voting day comes along-and that day will come soon now-they will be held responsible for what has been.' done in Bonaventure county in the last five yearn.
I think some pressure should be brought to bear on the administration of the Canadian National Railways to give the people on the Gaspe coast their fair share of the work that is being done. That is the second point.
The third point is as regards the purchase of railway ties. A few days ago I wrote to Mr. Hungerford, asldng for information in regard to all tenders for ties in Bonaventure county .and the reply I .received, which was similar to the reply given the year before, was that it was contrary to the public interest to give figures, but he gave me the figures for the previous year. The people of St. Charles de Caplan, St. Alphonse de Caplan, New Richmond and Bonaventure, and all that district where these ties are being bought, claim that they are underpaid. They say that the price paid the contractors is out of proportion to what is received by the farmers who supply these ties. The claim is that the fanners are not getting a fair price. Is that so? I am not in a position to say, but as the representative of that county I think that when we are called upon to vote millions of money to a company who refuse to give us elementary information-, we have a right to protest, because we are entitled to have that information.
This is another instance of the ill feeling which is being created in that part of the country against the administration of the Canadian National Railways. I do not want to blame the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart, Leeds) at the present time for the very extensive outlay that he is and has been carrying on in the county of Bonaventure in the last four years. Public wharves that have been built in my time during the last thirty years are being improved in order to bring them to a state of efficiency, and in addition to that he is building a number of new public wharves. Those wharves of course will be required for water transportation, but the water transportation there works contrary to the interest of the Canadian National Railways, and that railway will probably show a large deficit this year as it did the year before on the administration of the Gaspe line. I cannot protest against those wharves being kept in repair and others being built if they are necessary, but if such large amounts are being spent to enable water transportation to be carried on, surely something should be done in the interest of the railways and of their employees as well as in that of the people who look to the government to have their interests in this connection protected. Of course the answer is a very poor one, but the minister I understand cannot do otherwise than say that the administration of the road rests with the commission, which is a creation of parliament; but I would not be doing my duty did I not bring these grievances to the attention of the house.

Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada, and to authorize the government to guarantee equipment securities of the Canadian^ National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the amount of fifteen million dollars.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Morand in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
the desirability of relieving unemployment through the construction of public works has been so generally advocated and so universally accepted that I trust this resolution is not a controversial one in any sense. The house at its last session provided in round figures the sum of S40,000.000 to be expended on projects set forth in the schedule to the act known as the Public Works Construction Act, 1934. That act was passed about the end of June and works were undertaken where possible, particularly out of the general vote, during the last season. Plans had to be prepared and tenders invited, and on the 31st of March last, although the winter season had intervened and stopped construction practically entirely, there had been expended and earned the sum of approximately $10,000,000, leaving in round figures about $30,000,000 of the amount appropriated under that act still unexpended. Tenders have been invited and works undertaken on practically all of the larger projects in that schedule, so that it is fair to assume that during this year the larger part of the remaining $30,000,000 unexpended will be earned under the act of 1934.
A large number of men have been employed in putting buildings in repair, on improvements, and in actual construction work, and the building trades undoubtedly have been very much helped in this connection. It has been stated, and I think fairly accurately, that for each man employed on the actual con-

Public Works Program
stru-etion of a building you may assume that there are three others employed who do not actually appear upon the building.
Now it is deemed expedient to supplement the program of works undertaken last year under the act of 1934, and a bill based upon the resolution which has just been submitted to the committee will be introduced immediately upon the adoption of this resolution. There is in the resolution the added feature covering the guarantee of the securities of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway to the amount of $15,000,000 for the purchase of equipment, and the details of that will be set out in the bill. The same object and the same purpose is served in both these projects-the employment of labour. As the matter is not controversial I suggest that we adopt the resolution, after I have given such additional information as the committee may require at this stage, and immediately upon its adoption the bill which has been prepared will be introduced. I am convinced that members are all possibly more interested in the schedule of the bill than in the terms erf the resolution.

Mr. Hanbury: Would you make that statement again?
Mr. Heaps: Speak a little louder.
Mr. Hungerford: I say, in general we have lots of equipment, surplus of equipment, but again there are peak periods and it is during that time that all railroads may be short of a particular class of equipment for a short period of time.
Mr. Hanbury: How do you prepare for that shortage ?
Mr. Hungerford: We borrow from somebody who has it to spare. We all borrow and lend equipment as between railroads.
Mr. Tummon: That is the practice of all railroads?
Mr. Hungerford:	Yes, sir.
Mr. Hanbury: You never have any difficulty in taking care of the peak in that way?
Mr. Hungerford: No, not for many years.
I repeat there will be no attempt and there has been no attempt in any way, shape or form to force the Canadian National Railways to do anything which is not economically sound or correct.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Did they ask for this?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: They asked for equipment a long time ago. Some time ago they suggested equipment requirements on certain financial conditions.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: On what terms?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
They suggested that we
pay one-third of the total cost, and stated that if the government would absorb one-third they could economically carry the other two-thirds. My submission is, although I have not figured it out, that that is what we are doing to-day. If the notes are sold on a three and a half per cent basis we carry the principal-the principal is not repayable for two years-the interest is paid by the government for two years, and the Canadian National railway is charged up with something the government really pays in the end. I repeat the Canadian National Railways are going to be in the position of saying as to whether or not on this basis they will take equipment. No force or pressure is being used upon them, and at the present time they have not given a definite reply as to whether or not they want the equipment on these terms.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Although I appreciate the
frankness with which the minister has answered I am not prepared to admit that when a bill is introduced and passed through the house providing for a substantial loan to the Canadian National Railways to buy equipment it is not a very strong means of coercing them into buying,' whether they want it or not. In this connection I should like to refer to the report of the Duff commission. During the debate on March 16, 1933, in connection with the Canadian Pacific-Canadian National bill, I quoted paragraph 146 of the Duff report, as follows:
Of direct political interference by ministers and members of parliament in the detail operations of the railway, we were assured by the officials there -was little or none. It was in the larger sphere of policy that political considerations led to unwise and unnecessary capital expenditures, the result of which was to create an atmosphere in which the ordinary principles of commercial operation of the railway were lost sight of.
I was pointing out at the time this bill was being discussed that it had been heralded throughout Canada that this bill was to do away with political interference when in fact it did not do away with political interference in matters of policy. In my humble opinion this is one instance in which there is political interference. I have no reason to doubt the minister when he says that he is not forcing the Canadian National to take this equipment but we have the evidence given only a few days ago by Mr. Hungerford, general manager of the road, to the effect that he does not require any new equipment. We now have a bill being introduced which provides that they will be able to purchase equipment on certain terms. I am not discussing the advisability or the soundness of the principle which is being laid down perhaps for the first time in connection with relief legislation, namely, that certain private corporations shall be assisted directly as that is another matter which may be discussed at some other time; my objection to this section of the bill is that the Canadian National Railways is being asked or is being invited-

speechtext: That is a far better word than "coerced."

speechtext: -being invited to sit in at the feast. The company is being induced to spend money which its chairman and president do not consider necessary.

speechtext:
They can refuse the invitation the same as you and I refuse an invitation to dinner.
Public Works Program

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: They can refuse the invitation but the minister is leaving them open to very strong pressure from people in high positions and from sectional, personal and political interests. I suggest to the minister that that is not a fair position in which to place the trustees and the management of the road. If they do not consider it necessary to purchase equipment I do not think the government should blazon it forth to the people of this country that they are willing to buy equipment whether or not the Canadian National officials are. I suggest to the minister that this matter should be given further consideration from the standpoint of the principle that there shall be no political interference with the Canadian National Railways. I think he would be well advised to look over these sections again before introducing them.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am more concerned with the work which might be given to employees of the railroads. Two or three times during this session I have asked questions of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in connection with new equipment for the railroads, especially for the Canadian National road. I do not want to prolong the discussion, but I should like to refer to the first question which I asked on January 21 of this year. This question is reported on page 16 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask a question of the Minister of Railways. I have under my hand four communications, two letters and two telegrams, from different associations of the Canadian National Railways employees in the city of Stratford, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I propose to read the shortest of the telegrams which will take only a moment. It is addressed to me at the House of Commons, and read's as follows:
"Press reports indicate that new equipment for Canadian National Railways may be constructed by private companies. Canadian National Railways employees protest such contracts as equipment can be advantageously constructed in Canadian National repair shops. Respectfully request that you use your influence for this work to be done by the Canadian National Railways in their own shops, whereby former employes may be returned to work. A reply would be appreciated.
J. Thomas."
I shall not read the rest of my question, but the minister's reply was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the same telegram I presume came to me among many others. There were many telegrams and letters from various sections of the country that were based upon a statement in the press which was not an official statement of any kind, and my reply to all the telegrams and letters has been that the matter has not been decided upon by the government; that there have been proposals put to the
f Mr. Manion.]
government for equipment by railway ear equipment companies, but that no decision of any kind has been arrived at.
On the following day, January 22, I put a further question to the Minister of Railways, which is reported on page 66 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) based on a telegram I received this morning from the city of Stratford. It is as follows:
"Lodge 103 International Association of Machinists at Stratford with over 400 members protests that contracts for new equipment for Canadian National Railways be let to private companies while railway shops have worked only sixteen days a month for the past three years.
W. Lyons,
Recording Secretary,
73 Dufferin Street, Stratford."
On February 25 I put another question to the minister, and again on March 18, but I shall not delay the committee by reading these questions. My object in putting these questions was to urge that this new equipment, including repairs, be constructed as much as possible in the Canadian National shops. While ordinarily it would be out of order, I submit that as the minister quoted from the evidence given before the standing committee on railways and shipping, I should be granted the same privilege. I should like to refer to something more recent than the questions which I put to the minister in the house. I have before me the minutes of the evidence of the select standing committee on railways and shipping for April 10, and I should like to quote from page 111, as follows:
Mr. Gray: Then I should like to ask the chairman of the board a question. I notice on page 6 of the analysis of operations there were no purchases of new equipment during 1934. There have been reports in the press, Mr. Chairman, and Mr. Sanderson in the House of Commons has asked questions from time to time, first on the 21st day of January, of the Minister of Railways, and he asked me to ask again with respect to this question of new equipment. There have been some newspaper suggestions that a large amount of money was to be spent for new equipment and that the orders were to be placed with private firms and that this would affect the Canadian National shops. The minister at that time was not able to give an answer.
Hon. Mr. Manion: I gave an answer that the matter had been submitted to us and was still under consideration by both ourselves and the railway company, and it is still in the same position to-day.
Mr. Gray: Is there any suggestion that there will be money spent?
Hon. Mr. Manion: There are lots of suggestions, particularly on the part of the Canadian railway equipment manufacturers, but there has been no decision arrived at. _
Mr. Gray: Is there anything in the budget?

Then on page 112, which I think the minister has put on the record, we find questions asked by Mr. Gray, Mr. Hanbury and Mr. Heaps. I will not take up the time of the committee quoting that. We find that the resolution before this committee, standing in the name of the Prime Minister, reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada, and to authorize the government to guarantee equipment securities of the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the amount of $15,000,000.
I find no fault with that at all. My sole concern is that if the government decide to assist the railways to the extent of $15,000,000,	$8,000,000 to the Canadian
National Railways and $7,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific, whether by loan or by guarantee-it makes no difference what it is -it will create a large amount of employment for the employees who make railway equipment of every kind; and I would strongly urge the minister, especially in connection with the Canadian National road, to insist that every dollar of the $8,000,000, or whatever the amount may be that is to be voted to the Canadian National for equipment, be paid to employees of the Canadian National Railways in Canadian National shops. I wish to put on the record some other communications I have received from the city of Stratford. I think it is my duty to do so because I feel very keenly in this matter. There is an opening here to assist, and assist greatly, the unemployed among the railway men.

speechtext:
Yes, I will be frank
with my hon. friend from Lincoln and say the city of Stratford, and I have no apologies to make, none whatever. I want to put on the record a telegram I received dated Stratford, Ontario, January 18, 1935:
Press reports indicate owing to economies by railway management, railway equipment and locomotives need to be replaced by new equipment. Respectfully point out that large amount of such economies were made possible by many employees being laid off and others placed on reduced work hours. Respectfully request that if new equipment needs to be constructed that such work be done in our railroad shops where there is now ample accommodation to do such 92582-174
work and thus return to the laid off employees their jobs and those now working 128 hours per month again resume 40 hours per week. Above is copy of resolution sent to Dr. Manion.
Your hearty support and influence in the house requested. Please reply.
Russell,
C.N.R. Local Federated Crafts, 116 Ontario street, Stratford.
I also received two letters and I hope it will not weary the committee if I put these on the record. The first is dated January 19, 1935:
Dear Sir,
Press reports indicate that there is to be considerable construction of new railroad equipment in the near future. Our members wish to draw to your attention their claims for having this work done in our own shops.
During the past four years our members in main shops have, in an effort to avoid the laying off of men, been voluntarily working less than 30 hours per week when our agreements entitled them to claim a minimum of 40 hours per week. This was agreed to by the men. many of them knowing that this sacrifice would cause considerable hardship to themselves and their families. Many have lost their life savings which were invested in homes and many more are anxiously looking for improved conditions in order to avoid this hardship. We feel therefore that we are not being unreasonable when we ask that all orders for new equipment should be placed in our own shops on the C.N.R., they being quite capable of taking care of this work without additional overhead costs of supervision, etc.
Trusting that we can count on your influence and support and assuring you that a reply would be appreciated' by our members, I am,
Yours truly,
K.	Cockburn,
Secretary.
I have another letter dated January 18, 1935:
Dear Mr. Sanderson:
I have on behalf of our local organization forwarded the following night letter to Hon. Dr. R. J. Manion, Minister of Railways:
"Press reports indicate that owing to economies by railroad managements, railroad equipment and locomotives need to be replaced by new equipment.
Respectfully point out that large amount of such economies were made possible hy many employees being laid off and others placed on reduced working hours.
Respectfully request that if new equipment is needed that work be done in our railroad' shops where there is now ample accommodation to do such work, and thus return to employment the laid off employees and restore the forty hour week to those now working less than an average of thirty hours per week?'
Railway Carmen of Stratford, Ont.
The members of our organization would request that you help them in every way, to make possible their desires as outlined in above request.
Respectfully yours,
F. J. Cullum
For Stratford Lodge No. 928.

Public Works Program

As I said to my hon. friend from Lincoln, I have no apologies to make for putting these letters on the record. I would strongly urge on the minister that the $8,000,000 in connection with the Canadian National be spent in the shops.
I want to ask the minister a question, and I do not need a reply now; it will be satisfactory if he will be good enough to answer when I get through with my remarks. Has he any estimates as to the equipment required? For instance, can he tell the committee how much money will be spent on, say, repairs to old equipment? Has he any estimate of the amount that will be spent on entirely new equipment in the shops?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I did say earlier in my remarks that we should probably ask the two railways to give about $3,000,000 of this money for repairs in their shops throughout Canada.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I wish now to say a word or two with regard to railway matters generally, because I think that this is an appropriate time to discuss to some extent at least the great railway problem of Canada. I believe that all hon. members will agree with me when I say that the railways in this country present one of the most vital problems that face the taxpayers of Canada. We have two railway systems, one publicly owned and one a privately owned system. Perhaps I can say without fear of contradiction that in these two railway systems we have the two best in the world. I do not think I am at all exaggerating when I make that statement. During the last four or five years both these railways have been carrying on under great difficulties, but their difficulties are no greater comparatively than those of every business firm, every industrial concern in the dominion. I think I can go further and say that comparatively their difficulties are no greater than those of the individual, no matter in what business he may be engaged. In my opinion the railway industry of this country is its second greatest. I do not think it is the first, because I would put the great basic industry of agriculture first, but I do regard our railways as the second greatest industry in Canada. If we stop to consider the business that these railways are doing, we see that under normal conditions the Canadian National uses 22,000 miles of track and the Canadian Pacific Railway 18,000; and combined, when traffic is normal, they employ 190,000 men with an annual pay roll of $290,000,000. That includes salaries and wages, and that pay roll of $290,000,000 sustains almost 1,000,000 people. That will give you some idea of the immensity of the railway system in Canada. But both railways

lack one thing at present; they lack the normal tonnage in traffic, going back to the twenties. I have no hesitation in putting myself on record this afternoon, that when normal conditions return in this country, as they will, both these railways will have solved all their difficulties; and when revenue and traffic increase the deficits will automatically be wiped out, and we shall not hear very much criticism of the railways. Go back ten years ago; there was no criticism of the railways then. They were doing well; their earnings were large and they were employing a very large number of men. They were in the same condition as all business was at that time-they were what we called prosperous. I repeat that when normal conditions return to this country the railways will be able to take care of themselves without very much assistance.
I am not going into the financial structure of the Canadian National Railways or ancient history .as to how all those conglomerations of roads were brought into the national system, but I say that if we have patience; if we preserve the railway intact and if we do not allow any insidious and vicious propaganda to undermine it, when we come out of our difficulties, the Canadian National will be one of the great assets of our people. We should be proud of the Canadian National Railways and we should also be proud of the Canadian Pacific Railway; they are both assets to the country. But there is a propaganda being spread throughout Canada to undermine and if possible injure the publicly owned road. I know that the minister does not assume any responsibility for that; as a matter of fact he stated on the floor of the house not more than two weeks ago, when speaking on Canadian National affairs generally in regard to the amalgamation or unification of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, that the government of which he is Minister of Railways is opposed to anything of that nature. I put the question to him myself and he was good enough to permit the question and to reply. He said that he was speaking for the government. I asked him a second question, if he were speaking for the Prime Minister, and he was good enough to reply that he was. Of course I must take his answers as he gave them to me. But apart altogether from that, a very eminent gentleman, an outstanding man, is going throughout the dominion spreading propaganda to injure and is injuring the Canadian National: I refer to the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I want to point out to the Minister of Railways and to the government that they are the directors of the Canadian National

Public Works Program
system for the people, for the taxpayers of this country, and as regards this propaganda that is being spread-and apparently no effort is being made by the government to combat or contradict or stop it-I think their duty is to combat that propaganda.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I do not think I should
let my hon. friend make that statement, because within the last four or five months I have made at least three statements, one in Smith's Falls, one in Brockville, and one in this house, in all of which I have taken absolutely the opposite standpoint from that taken by Mr. Beatty. I have done everything in my power to combat the propaganda.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I accept the minister's statement in good faith and I think he is sincere, but I believe I can tell him something he should do. At the head of the Canadian National board we have Judge Fullerton. He has made one speech mildly contradictory of the speeches that Mr. Beatty has been making throughout the whole dominion. The minister said this afternoon when a certain bill was up, before this resolution came before the house-I think it was this and if I am wrong, the minister will correct me-that he never did anything to interfere with Mr. Fullerton making speeches on behalf of the Canadian National system, speeches that would be contradictory to and combating those of Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Am I right in that?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Well, it has been stated in the Winnipeg Free Press, as quoted by the hon. member-and I saw an editorial in a newspaper which is usually much fairer than the Winnipeg Free Press, making the same statement-that we had in some way prevented Mr. Fullerton from making speeches. I pointed out that Mr. Fullerton was at liberty to make any speeches he chose, and in no manner, shape or form, did we interfere; but I quoted1 Mr. Fullerton as stating in the committee last year that he did not consider that he had any right to get into a controversy with Mr. Beatty regarding amalgamation, and he was approved in that by two members of the committee from my hon. friends side of the house.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I accept the statement of the minister, but does he not think it is the duty of the government of the day, and of himself as Minister of Railways, to instruct Mr. Fullerton, or someone who has responsibility in regard to the publicly-owned system which is controlled more or less by the government of the day, to go out and combat the propaganda that Mr. Beatty is putting out?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I have no power to instruct Mr. Fullerton. He is the chairman of the board of trustees of the Canadian National. Certainly I think if misstatements of fact are made about the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Fullerton should correct them, but it is debatable, and apparently it was not the opinion of the committee last year that Mr. Fullerton and Mr. Beatty should be travelling around the country carrying on an amalgamation and anti-amalgamation vendetta on the public platform. But I have no power to instruct Mr. Fullerton. My own opinion was that the feeling for amalgamation in this country was so slight that in spite of Mr. Beatty's arguments for it there was no great body of public opinion favourable to it at the present time.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Well, again I accept the statement of the minister. But if he says he has not the authority to instruct Mr. Fullerton, and perhaps he has not, surely in the interests of the Canadian National system he should advise him that some steps should be taken to combat Mr. Beatty's propaganda. I would put Mr. Beatty in this category, as far as his propaganda against the Canadian National Railways is concerned: I would call him "public enemy No. 1." He has no right to do it, and I do not think he should be permitted to do it.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: How would he be stopped?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Let me go on to explain. It would be bad enough for any private citizen-

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Section 98.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes, or he might do it under peace, order and good government. This government can do almost anything under peace, order and good government.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: And do it well.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: If they do not know of any other method, it might be under peace, order and good government.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That was struck out of the act at your suggestion.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Oh, no. Mr. Beatty
has been spreading this propaganda over the country for the last four years. He should be the very last man to be permitted to go about the country attacking the Canadian National. It would be bad enough for any private citizen to do that, but it is even worse that the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the privately owned road, the chief competitor of the Canadian National, which is owned by the people, paid for and financed by the tax-
Public Works Program

payers, should go about systematically attacking the credit and the structure of and everything pertaining to the Canadian National. Some effort should be made to stop it. It is not fair to the people of Canada, it is not fair to the Canadian National Railways, and it is most unfair to the vast army of employees of the Canadian National.
What is Mr. Beatty's object? I think I would be safe in saying that in this propaganda Mr. Beatty's object is to bias and prejudice the minds of the people in regard to their own railroad. He is doing all the injury he can to the publicly owned road. I hope I am fair in saying that I think his object is to depreciate as much as possible the people's road so that when the time comes he as president and manager of the privately owned road can gobble up the publicly owned road at his own price and we shall have but one railroad system in this country. I think that is Mr. Beatty's object.
In regard to amalgamation or unification, so far as I am concerned I am absolutely opposed to it.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I am absolutely opposed to any system of any kind that will unite these two railroads.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
We want the two
railroads in this country.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Either under government
or under private ownership?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Absolutely. We want the privately owned road and we want the publicly owned road, both serving the people.
A few years ago there was very little criticism regarding the Canadian National. I want to put on record something that the Prime Minister said in regard to the Canadian National back in August, 1926. Perhaps I did put this on record at one time, but I think it will bear repeating. The occasion was a political meeting in the city of Stratford at the time of the election of 1926. Mr. Bennett was not the Prime Minister then; I think he was Minister of Finance in the Meighen government. He was in Stratford addressing a large audience, most of them employees of the Canadian National, and he is reported in the Toronto Globe of August 16, 1926, in the Toronto Mail and Empire of the same date, the London Advertiser, the London Free Press and the Stratford Herald, all of August 16. The meeting was held on August 14, which was a Saturday night, consequently the report in the papers was two days later. This is what Mr. Bennett said:

Mr. Bennett denounced' in scathing terms the whispering campaign about the Canadian National Railways, saying that Mr. Meighen had always fought for the road, and had no intention of interfering with its management. In that connection he said that he personally had recommended to Mr. King that Sir Henry Thornton be hired to operate the road. This he had done as a result of information from Mr. Thomas in England, he said, and indicated' that he thought Sir Henry Thornton had been successful and that his work would certainly not be interfered with by Mr. Meighen.
I read this at the present time for this purpose; I do not think there is any man in this country who has more influence over Mr. Beatty than the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister should try some of this discipline stunt on Mr. Beatty. He uses it in politics. I do not want to be unkind to the Prime Minister, but I think he has it in his power to stop the propaganda that Mr. Beatty is spreading in regard to the Canadian National road. Apparently the Prime Minister has changed his mind to some extent in regard to the Canadian National. I would refer the committee to Hansard of March 9,1933, pages 2853 and 2854. The Prime Minister at that time was speaking on Bill No. 37, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific bill, and he is reported in Hansard as follows:
I am going to make a very short review of the situation, Mr. Speaker, and of the legislation now before the house, and I think I can convince hon. members opposite that they are approaching this question from, shall I say, the wrong angle. The position is not, as has been suggested so frequently in this house, that these are the properties of the people of Canada.
That from the Prime Minister! I will repeat it:
The position is not, as has been suggested so frequently in this house, that these are the properties of the people of Canada. These are now the properties of the people who loaned their money to build them, and under normal conditions they would take possession of them. It does seem to me that there are a few fundamental ideas which must be kept in mind in discussing these proposals. Let us look at them.
And then he goes on. I want to point this out to the committee, that the Prime Minister at that time, March 9, 1933, classed the Canadian National in the same category as the Canadian Pacific. He virtually said they were bankrupt. He virtually said they could not pay their debts. He virtually said that the Canadian taxpayer had not a dollar of equity in the Canadian National. Now that is not true; that is not correct. I want to say here, Mr. Chairman, that one of the greatest assets this country has is the publicly owned road, the Canadian National. Give it time and it will work out of its difficulties. I

Public Works Program
disagree entirely with the Prime Minister when he makes that statement of March 9, 1933, and I have very grave doubts whether he would repeat it to-day, that the Canadian National is bankrupt and that the people have no longer any equity in it. Such a statement as that from the Prime Minister at least does not enhance the Canadian National; it injures it. I do not for a moment say, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister made that statement of March 9, 1933, to injure the Canadian National Railway, but I say that it was a statement which as Prime Minister he should not have made, and to be as fair to him as possible I would say that it was bad judgment when he made that statement on the floor of the house on March 9, 1933. I have perhaps gone on longer than I should have, Mr. Chairman, but I wanted to put myself on record in regard to this resolution.

speechtext: No. Mr. Chairman, I urge again upon the minister in regard to this new equipment for the Canadian National Railway that not one dollar of this expenditure be handed out to private companies, but that work be given to Canadian National Railway employees and the work be done in the Canadian National Railway shops. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up more than two or three moments but I wish to say a few words in reply to my hon. friend and some others. In the first place, there has been and is now no coercion so far as the Canadian National
is concerned. Secondly, there has been no haste because as the hon. gentleman has pointed out, and as I have already told him, the matter has been under consideration for many weeks, and indeed I think many months. Thirdly the amount that was discussed in the newspapers and to which reference was made by my hon. friend and others was $80,000,000, and of course that was a ridiculous figure.
In regard to repairs in the shops there was the question not only of the workmen in the railway shops, and no one has more sympathy with them than I have, but there was also the whole question of the advisability of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, if you will, going into the manufacture on a huge scale of rolling stock for the railways. I pointed out earlier that it is the intention of the government, and it has been made clear to both railways in connection with this proposal, which was really a proposal originally from them-or rather a proposal was originally made by them both although not exactly on these lines, that we would like if they accepted this proposal to use at least twenty per cent of the whole thing in repairs, which would mean an increase in the amount of work for the railway shop men throughout the country. It is true it would not give them full time, but it must not be forgotten that the shop men on the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific have been receiving a good deal of work, certainly not full time but still a good deal of work, whereas the employees of the various railway equipment manufacturing plants throughout the country, of which there are five, three car manufacturing plants and two locomotive plants, have been given practically no employment now for a period of five years or more. These railway equipment manufacturing plants having been originally opened up, I am informed, at the solicitation of both railways many years ago, their employees also deserve some consideration. Therefore it was the opinion of the government and is my own opinion at the moment that the employment which this will provide should be divided up somewhat along the lines I have suggested.
I have only one more remark to make because I do not wish to delay some of my hon. friends from speaking, but I felt that a few of the statements that have been made should be replied to forthwith. In regard to the statement of the Prime Minister which my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) quoted, I assume that what was in the right hon. gentleman's mind, and what was clear enough in most people's minds, was
Public Works Program

that if it were not for government guarantees and for the government supplying money the Canadian National would go into the hands of a receiver, which it undoubtedly would. If the Canadian government had not been giving to the Canadian National for many years huge sums of money to make up the deficit on their bonds, undoubtedly the Canadian National would have gone into the hands of a receiver. I think it is clear enough that that is what was in the Prime Minister's mind; I do not think that is any reflection upon the Canadian National, and it is certainly no perversion of the facts. If it were not the practice of the government of Canada to-day, and if it had not been the practice for many years, to pay the deficits on the interest to the bondholders of the Canadian National, undoubtedly the bondholders would have been able to put the Canadian National into a receivership. Just as to-day, if the Canadian Pacific were unable to pay the interest on its bonds, the Canadian Pacific would be placed in the hands of a receiver. That is what the Prime Minister meant, and I do not think his words could be twisted into any implication of hostility on the part of the Prime Minister to the Canadian National. I do not think that they should be twisted in that way. I am not reflecting upon the hon. member, but I do not believe the Prime Minister meant anything other than what I have just said he meant.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

Perhaps some hon. members will be disappointed when I say I have no intention whatsoever of discussing the amalgamation of railways. It has been so definitely stated on many occasions by the minister that the government will adhere to its resolution, "amalgamation never, competition ever," and as it has also been stated as a policy of the Liberal party that they will endeavour to continue the Canadian National Railways as a separate organization, I am not at all disposed to quarrel with either party or to enter into any controversy at this time.
May I say this, however; in his first radio speech the Prime Minister said that the solution of the railway problem is precedent to the return of prosperity. In other words, we cannot have prosperity until the railways question, whatever that question may be, has been settled. Now, the Prime Minister has promised prosperity, and if he was sincere in bis promise then it certainly becomes his duty to enunciate some policy looking to the settlement of the railway problem. Yet in addressing the board of trade of the city of Toronto, after discussing for ten or fifteen minutes the difficulties in which the Canadian

National Railways found themselves, he is reported to have said, "But this is not Bennett's problem; it is your problem. What are you going to do about it?" I wish merely to point out the inconsistency of bringing in reform policies which are to have the effect of bringing back prosperity, and yet doing nothing to settle a question which the Prime Minister himself has said must be settled before we can have prosperity. The hon. member for South Perth in his very eloquent plea-

Now, a word with regard to the proposed vote of S15,000,000 towards purchasing equipment for the two railway companies, $8,000,000 of which is to go to the Canadian National Railways and $7,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway. 'Certainly I would not be heard advocating anything which would interfere with the giving of employment or relief to unemployed people. I think there is a decided difference between helping ourselves and helping somebody else. At the moment however I shall not discuss that point.
Just five days ago-I believe it was last Wednesday-the president of the Canadian National Railways appeared in committee and said, "We do not need any equipment; we have sufficient equipment for all our traffic requirements." That was the very definite and unqualified statement he made. He did say however that although they had plenty of cars and plenty of equipment for all general purposes there were periods of peak loads when the equipment was not Sufficient. "Then," h.e said, "We do as other railways do; we follow the very logical course of borrowing from the other roads. We exchange; we get cars from other roads when we need them, and they do the same when they find themselves in a similar position." My point is this:	If the Canadian

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) in connection with the financial history of the Intercolonial railway both before and after its inclusion in the Canadian National Railway system'. I think this statement is well worthy of being recorded in the journals of this house. I was also interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). I always enjoy the hon. gentleman's speeches, whether they be in earnest or otherwise, but in my judgment the speech he made to-day was purely partisan propaganda and rather unworthy of him. Both the hon. member for Quebec South and the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) took full advantage of the lack of relative responsibility which attaches to hon. members of the opposition. I would direct the attention of both hon. members to the statement which appeared this morning in the press with regard to the quantity of rolling stock, originally costing about $27,587,106, most of which will never again be put in
Public Works Program

service. This statement is attributed to the general manager of the Canadian National Railways. It is stated that from Sydney to Vancouver there are distributed some
16,000	to 20,000 cars which will never again see service. There are- a number of derelict locomotives which are useless and should be scrapped. Many of the locomotives in service to-day are expensive to operate because of the low boiler pressure under which they work.
While I do not claim that all the equipment referred to should be replaced at once, much of it must foe renewed if the Canadian National system is to maintain the service which it is exacted to give. The hon. member for South Perth was quite within his rights in acting as champion of the shop employees of the Canadian National Railways, but I would point out that none of these shops are in a position or ever were in a position to build locomotives or rolling stock in competition with the private shops. These shops are located in Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario, and with their private initiative they are able to produce rolling stock at a lower cost than can the ill equipped shops of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific. This has been proven time and time again. It is my well considered opinion that tihe equipment program now being presented by the minister is entirely inadequate. In the interests of the country I think it should be doubled, because this is the time to bore with a really big auger.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should
like to say a word or two on behalf of the citizens of the town of Transcona. When the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental railways were built a location some six miles from Winnipeg was chosen as the nucleus of their operations and the site of their shops. The largest and the most up to date railroad shops in the Dominion of Canada were built at this location. When running at full capacity these shops employ some 7,000 men but to-day only some 1,700 are employed. Many hundreds of men came to Transcona, bought property and built homes for themselves. As the hon, member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) indicated this afternoon, only a very small percentage of shop employees are employed at the present time, and these men are working only three days a week. I understand that the government intends to spend some $8,000,000 for replacements of one kind and another for the Canadian National Railways. I have been told that I can say without hesitation that there is not an item

of rolling stock which the shops at Transcona cannot produce. These shops have turned out pullman cars and have assembled engines, while it is the regular everyday task to build a freight car. In the early days of the history of the Canadian National Railways many men were prompted to go to Transcona. They built homes and cast in their lot with that town, but many of them have lost everything they had. I take this opportunity of appealing to the minister to ask that as large a proportion as possible of this money be spent upon equipment to be built at Transcona. I am not asking that these shops foe given priority over any other Canadian National shops, but I do ask that in the expenditure of this money these employees who have lost their all should receive serious consideration.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not
my intention to deal with matters connected with the Canadian National Railways, as these have already been dealt with in detail, but I should like to refer to the resolution itself. If this resolution contemplates a bill along the lines of the public works construction bill of last year, it will meet with strenuous objection on the part of members of this house. I do not know whether the minister would feel like giving us any information as to whether the bill will be drafted along the lines of the bill of last year. If he does, I should like to have some information in connection with the lump sum feature, then with regard to the power to put in other new buildings, and the inviting of tenders instead of having tenders by public advertisement.. These are some of the features in regard to which the minister might give me some information, which might have the effect of curtailing the remarks I desire to make. Is it intended to follow last year's action in these respects?

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I thought I intimated in my address when opening the discussion on this resolution that in a general way the terms of the bill were similar to those of the Public Works Construction Act of last year. The total amount involved is approximately $18,000,000 outside of the amount which would be provided for the railway guarantees and which would probably be $1,050,000-

-and, in addition, the $30,000,000 which we propose to spend under the former act, which would make a total of about $50,000,000 this year. The bill itself will disclose its provisions, and

Public Works Program
possibly when my hon. friend reads it he will find that his alarm may not be warranted, I am not prepared to discuss in detail the provisions of the bill until it is brought down, but again I assure my hon. friend that it is substantially the same as last year's, with a much shorter schedule.

maintopic: WORKS, UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEES OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: If it is substantially the same as last year's, I must say that it will not be very satisfactory in many respects. First of all, the amount is a large one. The minister has said -that it is practically $50,000,000.
